program.merge_policy: accumulate twenty 25-finding passes; consolidate, admit, validate, and merge once after Wave 2000

source_provenance: Sider Scholar + NCBI PubMed exact-source verification
repository-wide PMID collision screening using the Waves 1501-2000 PMID index through Wave 1850

policy.validation_strategy: PMID-level dedupe/source verification during authoring; expensive repository-wide validation only after Wave 2000

waves.focus: Randomized 8-week study in 30 trained male swimmers found upper-body plyometric training improved performance in both training groups, while beta-alanine produced greater gains in selected power/endurance measures and altered testosterone, cortisol and IgA; co-training design prevents pure supplement attribution.

Placebo-controlled trial in 299 adults found 12 weeks of carnosine produced only selective age/sex-specific endurance signals and no consistent grip-strength benefit; overall effects were limited rather than broadly ergogenic.

Mechanistic review proposes beta-alanine/carnosine buffering and glutamine metabolism as interacting components of muscle-brain crosstalk, but the neuroprotection framework is largely mechanistic and requires direct human validation.

Narrative review identifies beta-alanine, caffeine and carbohydrate mouth rinse as better-supported ergogenic strategies while characterizing BCAA, citrulline, taurine and probiotics as less directly established for perceived-effort-mediated endurance effects.

Narrative review maps protein, caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrates and peptide-related supplements in older/Masters athletes; useful evidence mapping but not a substitute for intervention-specific systematic review.

Crossover trial in 12 untreated hypertensive men found six days of L-citrulline improved autonomic recovery and reduced resting/post-exercise blood pressure responses after high-intensity exercise; very small male-only study needs replication.

Review describes possible L-citrulline effects on exercise performance, protein synthesis and muscle metabolism but identifies major gaps around strategy, transport, mitochondria and gut-muscle mechanisms.

Perinatal review describes strong metabolic/NO rationale for L-citrulline but emphasizes that adequately powered clinical trials are still needed before routine maternal or neonatal use can be recommended.

Pediatric vascular review summarizes L-citrulline as an investigational nitric-oxide-supporting therapy in systemic/pulmonary vascular disease; disease-specific pharmacotherapy evidence should not be generalized to wellness supplementation.

Review suggests exercise plus L-citrulline may support vascular and muscle outcomes in postmenopausal/older women, but explicitly calls for larger high-quality RCTs and long-term clinical confirmation.

Phase-I study in 10 adults with MELAS found no dose-limiting toxicity across tested L-citrulline doses and exploratory cerebral-blood-flow increases, while high doses raised guanidino compounds; efficacy requires a placebo-controlled trial.

Multicenter 2x2 factorial RCT in 266 ICU adults found resistance training improved function and longer-term outcomes, whereas HMB only modestly improved phase angle and fatigue with no benefit on most outcomes and no synergy with training.

Systematic review/meta-analysis evaluates HMB added to resistance training in older adults across muscle quality, body composition and physical function; retain as category-level synthesis pending source-specific effect extraction.

Randomized crossover trial in 30 active older adults found creatine plus HMB during supervised multicomponent training improved mobility and selected metabolic outcomes versus placebo; combined supplements and exercise prevent component-specific attribution.

Pilot RCT in 21 adults with decompensated cirrhosis found HMB-containing oral nutrition did not significantly improve muscle mass or grip strength versus control, despite within-group improvements in phase angle, arm circumference and chair-stand time.

Thirty-day RCT in older adults with sarcopenia found HMB improved selected muscle measures and adding fructooligosaccharides produced larger intestinal-barrier/inflammatory changes; combination design and short duration limit inference.

Acute human muscle-biopsy study found HMB altered hundreds of transcripts related to protein turnover, amino-acid transport and signaling; transcriptomic response is mechanistic evidence, not proof of long-term functional benefit.

Double-blind crossover study in 24 hemodialysis patients found an HMB+BCAA+zinc medical food improved muscle-thickness/body-composition and selected inflammatory markers but not short-term physical performance; multi-ingredient evidence.

Secondary analysis of a 30-person crossover trial found nominal creatine+HMB effects on glutathione-centered redox measures that did not survive false-discovery correction; exploratory correlations should not be presented as established antioxidant benefit.

Double-blind RCT in 102 adults with obesity found a protein/CaHMB supplement preserved skeletal muscle and improved fat-loss measures during energy restriction versus maltodextrin, but protein co-formulation prevents isolation of HMB-specific effects.

Small nonrandomized study in older adults with obesity, T2D and MASLD found heterogeneous muscle-mass changes during HMB-containing nutrition and no statistically significant overall gain; authors characterize the result as negative and exploratory.

Double-blind crossover study in 17 low-caffeine-consuming men found 300 mg morning caffeine lowered perceived exertion but did not clearly improve repeated sprint, strength, jump, mood or physiologic outcomes under standardized chronobiological conditions.

Sleep-manipulation plus double-blind caffeine study in 41 adolescents found no clear practically meaningful average change in value-based risk decisions from caffeine, sleep restriction or their interaction.

Meta-analysis found caffeine was self-reported as a migraine trigger by about 12% of participants, but heterogeneity exceeded 95% and observational self-report cannot justify universal caffeine avoidance.

Meta-analysis of randomized studies found acute caffeine, especially above 100 mg, transiently increased intraocular pressure in healthy and glaucomatous populations; clinically relevant safety context for susceptible users.
